title: Courage 3 Heart Sutra
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona takes up the Heart Sutra, opening with a koan about sand in the eye that shows pain and feeling remain after clear view. Heigaku asks who practices Prajnaparamita in the story and finds the answer in Avalokiteshvara, the embodiment of compassion, rather than Shakyamuni, Manjushri, or Beyonce. Anna Thorn's account of nuns chanting the sutra at a women's conference in Vietnam leads into a reading of the five skandhas and emptiness as boundlessness, empty of separateness. Heigaku closes by handing out index cards and envelopes for a meditation that asks "What is it?" of each thought and of the space between breaths.
topics: Boundless Heart Sutra of Interbeing Wisdom Surpassing Perfection

sentences.text: I studied the koan, which was recommended by her teacher to get rid of all her views in order to be truly free of her response in the end.
Even if you understand perfectly, there is still sand in the eye.
While there are some components of the story that remain a bit murky, the end teaching is that pain still exists and feelings still exist after clear view.
*The Boundless Heart Sutra of Interbeing Wisdom Surpassing Perfection.
The Enlightening One of Compassion, when practicing deeply the perfection of wisdom, clearly experienced all five human aspects as empty of their own being, and thus relieved all suffering.
Oh student, does not differ from emptiness, emptiness does not differ from form.
That which is form is emptiness, that which is emptiness form.
The same is true of judgment impulses, conceptions, mental patterns, consciousness.
Oh student, all teachings are marked with emptiness.
They do not appear nor disappear, are not tainted nor pure, do not increase nor decrease.
Therefore in emptiness there is no form, no judgment impulses, no conceptions, no mental patterns, no consciousness.

No eyes, no ears, no nose, no tongue, no body, no mind, no color, no sound, no smell, no taste, no touch, no object of mind, no realm of eyes until no realm of mind consciousness, no ignorance and also no extinction of ignorance until no old age and death and also no extinction of it.
No suffering, no origination, no stopping, no path, no cognition, also no attainment.*
*With nothing to attain an enlightening one depends on perfection of wisdom and the mind is no hindrance.
Without any hindrance no fears exist.
Far apart from every inverted view one dwells in the perfect present.
In past, present and future all enlightened ones depend on perfection of wisdom and attain unsurpassed complete perfect enlightenment.
Therefore know the perfection of wisdom is the great transcendent focus, the great bright focus, the utmost focus, the supreme focus which is able to relieve all suffering and is true not false.
So proclaim the perfection of wisdom focus.
Proclaim the focus that says gone, gone, gone beyond, gone utterly beyond.
Rejoice in the awakening.*
The Heart Sutra is about Prajnaparamita, emptiness wisdom that surpasses perfection.
In the translation we chant, *Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva when deeply practicing Prajnaparamita clearly saw that all five aggregates are empty and thus relieved all suffering.*
Who is it that's practicing Prajnaparamita in this story?
Is it Shakyamuni Buddha?
That's not what it says.
It's not the god of wisdom, Manjushri.
It's not a king or the president or Beyonce.
The one deeply practicing Prajnaparamita, the discernment of form as emptiness and emptiness as form, in this story is none other than the embodiment of compassion herself, Avalokiteshvara.
"No eyes, no ears, no nose, no body, no mind" sound kind of scary.
But maybe with Guanyin as the authority recommending this perspective, we can summon the courage to look more closely.
If the spirit of compassion is going to relieve all suffering in all beings, shouldn't she be out feeding the poor or listening to a sick friend or something?
You bet she is.
And she is doing so with the recognition that she is not separate from them.

Anna Thorne, while director of the San Francisco Zen Center, described attending an international women's conference on Zen in Vietnam and hearing nuns from all over the world taking turns chanting the Heart Sutra as they do at home.
The Heart Sutra is widely regarded as the best known and most popular Buddhist sutra.
With such a diversity of voices, she observed, at any moment you might choose to stop and consider it, the Heart Sutra is probably being chanted somewhere in the world.
She also points out that the Heart Sutra is not a teaching we can grasp intellectually, but over time, with effort, we become intimate with the teaching.
There are many different translations of the five skandhas or aggregates that make up a human being, or maybe I should say that fail to make up a human being.
It's not that there is confusion among the translators as to what the words in Sanskrit mean.
Rather, it is disagreement about which one English word comes closest to capturing the meaning of each one.
So I will use the words that make the most sense to me at this time, which is different than six months or three years ago, and I'm sure it will change again soon.
The first skandha is forms, which we do call form, which is the physical world.
The second is judgment impulses, which we translate as sensations.
That's our initial reflex reaction to any sensation as positive, negative, or to be determined.
And conceptions, we call perceptions, that's the six senses.
The five that we traditionally think of as the senses, plus including the mind's identifying, recognizing, or naming.
The fourth is mental patterns, mental formations, such as worry, appreciation, ideas, decisions, items that are activated by inputs to the mind.
And finally consciousness, awareness of other stuff present in the mind.
The point in studying the skandhas is that any place you go to identify yourself, what you find there is not you.
What you find there is in a transient state that came about because of many, many causes interacting.
And what you find there fades into other conditions very quickly.
The same can be said for any other object you suppose exists in the world.
Our true original nature, our Buddha face, is the mind that sees the world before taking on all of the limitations that are caused by our life experiences.
Suzuki Roshi likens this to Big Sky Mind.
We say that the sky is empty, but yet it nourishes all of life.
This practice isn't about pushing away the experiences of our judgment and prejudices from our life.
If we do that, we're like a truck stuck in the mud that just gouges a deeper and deeper rut as it spins its wheels.
Anna Thorne also observes that hearing and reflecting on the teaching of emptiness, and I might add chanting it, by chanting the Heart Sutra, will open us up to meeting emptiness.
We can study the substantiality we assume by examining what is this in everything that arises.
The emptiness of the Heart Sutra is sometimes translated as boundlessness because, as it says, all these things in their own being are empty.
In other words, they are empty of isolation, empty of separateness.
That is why Guanyin practices emptiness, because it is the emptiness of being interconnected with all beings, and then what could there be but compassion?
While it takes courage to study emptiness, the study is also a reservoir of infinite courage that you can tap into.
Tapping into that courage starts with questioning the assumptions underlying fear.

Assumptions about our capacity, about harm, about the skandhas, about our bodies, about our desires, about how we define others and ourselves, about how we're going to react, and about whether we'll notice.
Please get up now.
Pick up an index card and a pen and select one of the envelopes.
Don't open it up just yet.
Just hold it gently and return to your seat.
You will want to adjust to a posture where you will be able to meditate and write and have a little privacy, and be able to hear me.
So good luck.
Now settle into a posture of meditation.
When a thought or perception arises, ask the question, "What is it?"
And inspect it gently.
It will dissipate, and when it does, return to your breath.
Maybe ask, "What is it of the space between your breaths?"
Importantly, be open to what answer arises.
This isn't a mental exercise to think and figure out what it is.
Don't create the answer.
Allow it to speak for itself.
What is it?
